system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2129-11-30 16:24:00 to 2129-12-02 17:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, and a history of Puestow procedure was admitted for acute-on-chronic abdominal pain lasting three weeks, associated with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The pain was described as a deep epigastric ache radiating to the left side and back, different from his usual pattern, and exacerbated by a symptomatic ventral hernia. He reported syncopal episodes with incontinence during severe pain, previously evaluated as likely pseudoseizures. Abdominal imaging showed no obstruction or free air. He was managed with IV fluids, pain control with IV then oral Dilaudid, and temporary dietary restriction. His insulin was adjusted due to hypoglycemia on admission, with Lantus reduced from 10 to 5 units at bedtime. He tolerated advancement to a regular diet, and his symptoms improved. He was discharged home with instructions to continue medications, follow up with his primary care provider, and attend scheduled mental health appointments.
problems: Diabetes with other specified manifestations, type II or unspecified type, uncontrolled
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
ABDOMINAL RADIOGRAPH PERFORMED ON ___.

Comparison is made with a prior study from ___ and a CT abdomen and pelvis
from ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Tachycardia and ventral hernia, question SBO.

FINDINGS:  Five images of the abdomen were performed including left lateral
decubitus and upright projections.  The bowel gas pattern is unremarkable
without evidence of ileus or obstruction.  Surgical clips are noted in the
right upper quadrant likely from prior cholecystectomy.  There is no evidence
of free air below the right hemidiaphragm or along the liver edge on the left
lateral decubitus view.  Lung bases appear clear.  Bony structures appear
intact.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of bowel obstruction or free air.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH PERFORMED ON ___

Comparison is made with a prior study from ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Tachycardia, question acute process in the chest.

FINDINGS:  Upright AP view of the chest obtained.  The lungs are clear
bilaterally.  No free air below the right hemidiaphragm.  Cardiomediastinal
silhouette is normal.  Bony structures are intact.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intrathoracic process.  No evidence of pneumoperitoneum.

HISTORY:  Abdominal pain and known hernia but with now diffuse abdominal pain.
The patient is status post Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy (Puestow
procedure) ___.

COMPARISONS:  Multiple prior CT exams from ___ and
___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT-acquired axial images were obtained through the abdomen and
pelvis with intravenous contrast only.  Coronal and sagittal reformations were
evaluated.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  Limited evaluation of lung bases
is unremarkable.  Post-surgical changes from prior Puestow procedure with
Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy and distal enteroenteric anastomosis are
again seen.  There is new dilatation involving the duodenum and proximal loops
of jejunum, which measure up to 4 cm in size and are fluid filled, but without
a clear transition point.  There does appear to be some tapering of the bowel
in the midline (2:44), with the more distal loops of small bowel appearing
largely decompressed with the exception of the enteroentero anastomotic site
which also appears air filled and slightly dilated, and may relate to the
side-to-side anastomosis.  While there is slight twisting of the mesentery,
this has not significantly changed from prior exams and there is no secondary
mesenteric induration or findings of a closed-loop obstruction.

Remaining intra-abdominal organs including the liver, spleen, pancreas with
diffuse calcifications and mild atrophy consistent with a known history of
pancreatitis, adrenal glands, and kidneys appear unremarkable.  No free air,
free fluid, or pathologically enlarged lymph nodes are identified.  The
patient is status post cholecystectomy.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  Air is noted within the large
bowel and there is reidentification of a transverse colon containing ventral
hernia with a 6-cm neck.  There are no secondary imaging findings of
obstruction or strangulation/incarceration.  Bladder is moderately distended. 
No pathologically enlarged pelvic lymph nodes are seen.

BONE WINDOWS:  No malignant-appearing osseous lesions.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Findings suggestive of mild-to-moderate proximal small-bowel obstruction,
likely partial, with no discrete transition point identified.

2.  Unchanged transverse colon containing ventral hernia with no other
secondary findings of obstruction or strangulation.

3.  Post-surgical changes from prior Puestow procedure with stable appearance
to sequelae of chronic pancreatitis.

NOTE:  Since ___, this patient has had a total of 17 CT abdomen and pelvic
examinations available in our PACS system.  A high index of suspicion for
ordering future CT exams (with preferential use of ultrasound, MRI, or plain
films)  should be used in the future to minimize patients cummulative radation

diagnoses.long_title: Major depressive affective disorder, recurrent episode, severe, specified as with psychotic behavior
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Ventral, unspecified, hernia without mention of obstruction or gangrene
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this bad stomach pain for a few days. It’s worse than usual. I was vomiting and my belly’s been bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned flailing and being combative earlier—was that part of the pain episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, when the pain hits hard, I kind of lose it. I don’t mean to. It’s like my body just reacts. I’ve had seizures before, but they think some are not real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. We’ll keep that in mind. You also have a history of pancreatitis and a ventral hernia—is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had that Puestow surgery years ago. And the hernia’s been there a while. It’s been bulging more lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve ordered a CT scan to check for possible bowel obstruction, since your symptoms suggest that might be happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bowel obstruction? Like my intestines are blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It could be partial—meaning not fully blocked—but still causing pain and vomiting. We’ll know more after the scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan is back. It shows a partial small bowel obstruction—your upper intestine is a bit swollen and dilated, but there’s no clear blockage point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? Do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since it’s partial and you’re passing gas, we can try non-surgical treatment. You’ll be on IV fluids, nothing by mouth for now, and we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable. But what caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to scar tissue from past surgeries, or possibly your hernia. The CT shows the hernia is still there, but it’s not strangulated—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the hernia didn’t cause the blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not directly. It’s unchanged from before. But we’ll keep an eye on it. For now, we’re treating the obstruction conservatively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s better. Still a little bloated, but I haven’t vomited since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’re going to try reducing your hernia manually today—it’s reducible, so we can push it back in safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. You might feel pressure, but we’ll stop if it’s too uncomfortable. It could help relieve some of the strain on your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just completed the manual reduction. The hernia went back in easily. You did great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt pressure, but it wasn’t bad. My belly feels a little flatter already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep you NPO a bit longer, but if you keep improving, we might start clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatric team also stopped by. They reviewed your history of depression and suicidal thoughts. They recommend continuing your current mental health meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been struggling with that. PTSD from old trauma, and bipolar. I’ve been sober for years, but the mood swings still hit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your meds are adjusted properly. They suggested adding mirtazapine for sleep and depression—okay if we start that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve taken it before. Helps me sleep and eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’ve been stable overnight, no pain, and you passed gas again. We’re going to start you on clear liquids—broth, apple juice—and if you tolerate that, move to a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat solid food today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see how you do with clears first. If no nausea or bloating in a few hours, we’ll advance you. Your pancreas needs careful management, so we’ll go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the clear diet. We’re switching you to a regular diet. Start small—maybe toast and chicken—and let us know if you feel any discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m hungry. Can I take my pancreas enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve updated your prescription to Pancreaze—three capsules with meals. It’s stronger than what you were on. Helps with digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, we’re adjusting some of your other meds. Simvastatin dose is lowered, and we’re adding haloperidol for mood stabilization, as recommended by psych.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Haloperidol? I’ve taken that before. Helps with the racing thoughts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’re keeping lorazepam available for anxiety, plus prazosin for nightmares—common with PTSD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the regular diet, your vitals are stable, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you start vomiting, can’t keep food down, or have worsening pain. Also, watch for fever, or if the hernia becomes hard or painful. Follow up with your surgeon and PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no heavy lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—nothing over 10 pounds until you see the surgeon. Keep walking daily, stay hydrated, and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thanks for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, and a history of Puestow procedure was admitted for severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Imaging revealed a partial small bowel obstruction without a clear transition point, along with a reducible ventral hernia. He was managed conservatively with NPO status, IV fluids, pain control, and manual hernia reduction. His psychiatric history, including depression and PTSD, was addressed with medication adjustments. By hospital day three, he tolerated a regular diet, remained pain-free, and was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans. No surgical intervention was required.
